The mechanism is fully verifiable from the diff.

judged_text: The "minimum token response" schema is effectively a no-op: both computed keys ([z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()]) evaluate to the same string "[object Object]" so the schema reduces to { access_token: z.string() }, and z.object strips unknown keys so the sync-provided expiry is silently discarded from tokenResponse.data (e.g. Office365 never receives a new expiry_date, so its credential is treated as perpetually expired and re-refreshed on every operation)

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. At runtime `z.string().toString()` is the string "[object Object]", so these do not create a dynamic “any string key” rule; they just define (and overwrite) a single literal property named "[object Object]". Since `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, any real expiry fields (e.g. `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, etc.) returned by the sync endpoint are discarded from `refreshTokenResponse.data`, matching the finding’s claim that expiry can be silently lost.
